[SYSTEMIC PATTERN] This issue appears across multiple promotional sections, indicating a content pattern of invented marketing terms without glossary support.
issues.suggestion: Add a glossary or plain-language definitions for unusual, invented, or figurative terms.
issues.description_technical: Content contains idiomatic and fictional phrasing such as "fools like us," "Most of us don't bite. Much." and invented product names without literal interpretation or glossary, failing WCAG 2.2 SC 3.1.3 and 3.1.4.
issues.why_simple: A user with a cognitive disability or limited vocabulary may not understand that "Most of us don't bite" is a joke, or what "MarStar," "Wookie," or "Martianic" mean.
issues.why_technical: SC 3.1.3 requires a mechanism for identifying definitions of unusual words; SC 3.1.4 requires a mechanism for identifying the expanded form of abbreviations. The absence of such mechanisms makes comprehension harder for users with reading or language processing disabilities. Note: SC 3.1.3 and 3.1.4 are AAA criteria; real-world impact is lower than AA/A failures.
issues.suggestion_technical: Provide a visible glossary link, use <dfn> or <abbr> elements with title attributes, or add a "What this means" plain-language summary near invented terms.

issues.element: Multiple repeated <a> link blocks with identical text and different href query parameters
issues.description: The same link text appears many times with different destinations in the promotional content area, making it hard for users to tell where each link goes.
issues.suggestion: Make each link's destination clear from its visible label, or group repeated links so their purpose is obvious.
issues.description_technical: Multiple links share identical visible text such as "10% off Crater Adventure," "Free Astronaut Ice Cream," and "Fly with a Wookie" but point to different query-string destinations. This violates WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.4 and creates cognitive load under SC 3.2.3.
issues.why_simple: A user with memory or attention difficulties may click the wrong link because the labels look the same even though they lead to different pages.
issues.why_technical: Consistent, distinguishable link text reduces working-memory demand. When identical text maps to different URLs, screen-reader users and users with cognitive disabilities cannot predict the outcome of activation. NVDA/JAWS link lists will show multiple indistinguishable entries.
issues.suggestion_technical: Add distinguishing context to each link (e.g., "10% off Crater Adventure — main promo" vs. "10% off Crater Adventure — sidebar"), use aria-label or aria-describedby to clarify purpose, or remove redundant duplicate links.

issues.element: Repeated <input class="search" name="query" placeholder="search" type="text"/> and <input class="control-search" type="submit"/>
issues.description: Multiple search forms with the same placeholder and class names appear on the page (e.g., in the header and repeated content regions), which can confuse users about which search box to use.
issues.suggestion: Provide visible labels and reduce duplicate search forms, or clearly associate each search form with its region.
issues.description_technical: The page contains at least three search inputs with identical placeholder text and no visible labels or landmarks to distinguish them, failing consistent identification and orientation expectations in SC 3.2.4.
issues.why_simple: A user with ADHD or memory impairments may type a query into one search box, then see another identical box and wonder whether their search was submitted or which one is the "real" search.
issues.why_technical: Components with the same function should be identified consistently. Multiple unlabeled search forms without programmatic or visual distinction reduce predictability and increase cognitive load. Screen reader users navigating by form fields will encounter multiple unnamed "search" inputs.
issues.suggestion_technical: Add a visible <label for="..."> for each search input, use aria-label or aria-labelledby to describe each search form's scope (e.g., "Search site" vs. "Search this section"), and remove redundant search forms if possible.

issues.description: Search inputs rely only on placeholder text and have no visible labels, making it harder for users to remember what the field is for after they start typing. [SYSTEMIC PATTERN] This issue appears in 3+ search inputs across the page, indicating a missing global form-label rule in the design system.
issues.suggestion: Add a visible, persistent label above or beside each search field.
issues.description_technical: The search inputs use placeholder="search" as the only visible label. Placeholder text disappears when the user types, and it is not a persistent label. This fails WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.2.
issues.why_simple: A user with a memory or attention disability may forget what they are supposed to type once the placeholder disappears.
issues.why_technical: SC 3.3.2 requires labels or instructions to be visible or programmatically associated and persistent. Placeholder text alone is not sufficient because it vanishes on input and has poor color-contrast persistence. JAWS/NVDA in Forms Mode will announce only "search" as the placeholder, which is not a robust accessible name.
issues.suggestion_technical: Wrap each search input in a <label> or use <label for="id">Search</label> with a matching id on the input. Do not rely on placeholder alone.

issues.element: <input class="search" name="query" placeholder="search" type="text"/> appears multiple times
issues.description: The same search field is repeated in different parts of the page, which may force users to re-enter information they already typed.
issues.suggestion: Ensure search query state is preserved across duplicate search forms, or consolidate them into one.
issues.description_technical: Multiple identical search forms without shared state could lead users to re-type queries. While the HTML alone does not prove state is not preserved, the repetition creates a redundant-entry risk under SC 3.3.7.
issues.why_simple: A user who already typed a search term may see another search box and think they need to type it again.
issues.why_technical: SC 3.3.7 applies to information entered in a process, not to a single search field repeated on a page. The repeated search inputs are a consistency/labeling issue (SC 3.2.4 / 3.3.2) rather than a redundant-entry barrier unless they are part of a multi-step process requiring re-entry.
issues.suggestion_technical: Use a single search form, or populate all search inputs with the current query value server-side or via JavaScript so users do not have to re-enter it.

issues.element: <video aria-hidden="true" playsinline="" tabindex="-1" webkit-playsinline=""> + <button class="ytp-unmute ytp-popup ytp-button ytp-unmute-animated ytp-unmute-shrink" style="display: none"></button>
issues.description: An embedded video player in the page content is present with no visible, easy-to-reach pause or stop control in the provided markup.
issues.suggestion: Provide visible, keyboard-accessible play/pause and mute controls for the video.
issues.description_technical: The video element is present but the only control found is a hidden unmute button. Auto-playing or hard-to-control media can violate SC 2.2.2 if it distracts users and cannot be paused.
issues.why_simple: A user with ADHD or anxiety may be distracted or overwhelmed by video that starts playing and is hard to stop.
issues.why_technical: SC 2.2.2 requires a mechanism to pause, stop, or hide moving, blinking, or scrolling content. A video without accessible, visible playback controls fails this requirement. VoiceOver/TalkBack users may not reach hidden controls via swipe navigation.
issues.suggestion_technical: Add native <video controls> or custom accessible controls with aria-labels (e.g., aria-label="Play", aria-label="Pause", aria-label="Mute") and ensure they are focusable and visible.

issues.element: <html lang="en"> page with no breadcrumb, no visible section headings hierarchy, and repeated content
issues.description: The page lacks breadcrumbs, a clear heading hierarchy, or other wayfinding cues, making it hard for users to understand where they are.
issues.suggestion: Add a breadcrumb trail and ensure headings clearly describe each section.
issues.description_technical:
No breadcrumb, site map link, or consistent heading structure is visible in the markup. Headings are repeated and some are empty (e.g.,

), reducing orientation support under SC 2.4.8.
issues.why_simple: A user with memory or cognitive disabilities may feel lost because there is no clear "You are here" indicator.
issues.why_technical: SC 2.4.8 requires information about the user's location within a set of Web pages. The absence of breadcrumbs, a visible current-page indicator, or a meaningful heading hierarchy makes orientation difficult. Note: SC 2.4.8 is AAA; the more impactful heading-structure issues are covered under SC 1.3.1 (screen-reader-17).
issues.suggestion_technical: Implement a visible <nav aria-label="Breadcrumb"> with an ordered list showing the path to the current page, and ensure each <h1>–<h6> has meaningful, non-empty text.

issues.element: Mars Commuter Express Terms and Conditions + links containing "USD", "GBP", "CAD"
issues.description: Currency and other abbreviations appear without expansion in the country/currency selector area, which may confuse some users.
issues.suggestion: Expand abbreviations on first use or provide a glossary.
issues.description_technical: The page includes abbreviations such as USD, GBP, and CAD in resident/currency selector links, and potentially other acronyms, without a mechanism to expand them. This may fail SC 3.1.4.
issues.why_simple: A user with a learning disability may not know that USD means United States Dollars, making the currency choice harder.
issues.why_technical: SC 3.1.4 requires a mechanism for identifying the expanded form of abbreviations. While common currency codes may be widely known, providing expansion reduces cognitive load for users with reading disabilities. Note: SC 3.1.4 is AAA and common currency codes have low real-world impact.
issues.suggestion_technical: Use <abbr title="United States Dollars">USD</abbr> or add plain-language labels such as "USD — United States Dollars".

issues.description: The page has no <title> element in the document head, so screen readers announce nothing meaningful when the page loads.
issues.suggestion: Add a descriptive <title> element inside <head> that identifies the page.
issues.description_technical: The document head is missing a <title> element, violating WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.2 (Page Titled).
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user hears only the URL or silence on load, with no clue what page they are on.
issues.why_technical: Screen readers announce the <title> as the first item when a page loads; its absence removes the primary orientation cue for assistive technology users. NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver all rely on <title> for initial page identification and browser tab navigation.
issues.suggestion_technical: <title>Mars Commuter - Book Your Trip to Mars</title>

issues.description: Search submit buttons in the page header and repeated search forms have no accessible name, so screen readers announce them only as 'button' or 'submit button'.
issues.suggestion: Add a value or aria-label describing the button's action.
issues.description_technical: The submit <input> elements lack value, aria-label, or aria-labelledby, leaving them without an accessible name per WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.2.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user cannot tell what the button does beyond 'submit'.
issues.why_technical: Without an accessible name, the button is announced generically, reducing efficiency and clarity for assistive technology users. NVDA + Firefox: announces "submit button" without action label; JAWS 2024: skips unnamed submit buttons in Forms Mode or announces generically.
issues.suggestion_technical: <input class="control-search" type="submit" value="Search"/> or <input class="control-search" type="submit" aria-label="Search"/>

issues.description: A country preference checkbox in the currency/resident selector area has no associated label, so screen reader users do not know what it controls.
issues.suggestion: Add a label describing the checkbox purpose.
issues.description_technical: The country preference checkbox has no <label for="id-country-preference">, aria-label, or aria-labelledby, violating WCAG 2.2 SC 1.3.1 and SC 4.1.2.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user hears only 'checkbox, unchecked' with no description of what it does.
issues.why_technical: Without a programmatically associated label, the checkbox lacks an accessible name and purpose in the accessibility tree. NVDA: announces "checkbox, not checked" with no name; JAWS 2024: skips element entirely in Forms Mode due to missing accessible name.
issues.suggestion_technical: <label for="id-country-preference">Set my country preference</label><input class="no-border" id="id-country-preference" name="country-preference" type="checkbox" value="1"/>

issues.description: The id 'id-country-preference' is used on more than one checkbox in the currency/resident selector area, breaking label associations and fragment navigation.
issues.suggestion: Ensure every id is unique across the page.
issues.description_technical: Duplicate id attributes violate WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.1; assistive technologies and browsers use the first match, ignoring subsequent duplicates.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user clicking the label may toggle the wrong checkbox, or the second checkbox may not be correctly identified.
issues.why_technical: Duplicate IDs break the one-to-one relationship required by id-based attributes such as for/id and aria-labelledby, causing unpredictable behavior. Browsers and AT resolve getElementById to the first match, so labels and aria-activedescendant may target the wrong control.
issues.suggestion_technical: Change the second checkbox id to a unique value and update any associated labels.

issues.description: An image in the page content has alt text that is a filename ('icecream.jpg') that does not describe the actual image content (a space station).
issues.suggestion: Replace the filename alt text with a description of the image's content and purpose.
issues.description_technical: The alt attribute contains a filename rather than a meaningful description, violating the intent of WCAG 2.2 SC 1.1.1.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user is told the image is 'icecream.jpg' when it actually shows a space station, which is misleading.
issues.why_technical: Filename-based alt text does not convey the purpose or content of the image and can confuse users relying on non-visual access. NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver will announce "icecream.jpg graphic" rather than meaningful content.

issues.description: An image in the page content has alt text that is nonsensical and unrelated to the actual image, which appears to be a Martian sunrise.
issues.suggestion: Write alt text that accurately describes the image.
issues.description_technical: The alt attribute does not describe the image content, violating WCAG 2.2 SC 1.1.1.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user hears a silly, unrelated phrase instead of what the image actually shows.
issues.why_technical: Alt text must be equivalent to the visual content; inaccurate alt text is worse than no alt text because it actively misleads users. VoiceOver iOS: "Beautiful baboon, blowing bubbles, biking backward, image" gives no indication of the Martian sunrise visual.

issues.description: A channel logo image in the embedded video section has generic alt text ('thumbnail-image') that does not identify the channel.
issues.suggestion: Use the channel name as the alt text.
issues.description_technical: The logo image uses non-descriptive alt text, failing to provide an equivalent text alternative per WCAG 2.2 SC 1.1.1.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user cannot tell which YouTube channel this logo represents.
issues.why_technical: Generic alt text such as 'thumbnail-image' does not convey the purpose or identity of the image, reducing navigational clarity. TalkBack: cannot identify the channel from the generic alt; VoiceOver rotor image list will show "thumbnail-image" with no context.

issues.description: Multiple links in the promotional content area have no visible or accessible text, so screen readers cannot announce their purpose.
issues.suggestion: Add descriptive text or an aria-label to every link.
issues.description_technical: Several <a> elements are empty (no text, no aria-label, no aria-labelledby, no img alt), violating WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.4.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user hears only the URL or 'link' with no clue where the link goes.
issues.why_technical: Empty links are exposed without an accessible name, making link lists and rotor navigation useless. NVDA link list: shows blank entries or raw URLs; VoiceOver rotor: lists "link" with no destination context; TalkBack: cannot determine link purpose via swipe navigation.
issues.suggestion_technical: Why MarsCommuter

issues.description: Image links in the promotional grid contain images with no alt text, so the link has no accessible name.
issues.suggestion: Add alt text to images inside links that describes the link destination.
issues.description_technical: Links wrapping images with empty or missing alt attributes have no accessible name, violating WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.4 and SC 4.1.2.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user hears only the destination URL or 'link' instead of a description of the linked promotion.
issues.why_technical: When a link contains only an image, the image's alt text becomes the link's accessible name; missing alt leaves the link unnamed. JAWS 2024: announces the href URL; NVDA link list: shows the raw URL; VoiceOver: double-tap may activate the link but user has no prior context.

issues.element: I'm a U.S. resident and/or I would like to book in USD.
issues.description: Country selector links in the currency/resident selection area are verbose and may be difficult to scan in a screen reader link list.
issues.suggestion: Use concise link text and add supplementary text outside the link if necessary.
issues.description_technical: The link text is long and conversational; while descriptive, it may hinder efficient scanning in rotor/link lists.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user browsing links hears a full sentence for each country option, slowing navigation.
issues.why_technical: Verbose link text is accessible but reduces efficiency; consider shorter link text with additional context if needed. This is a best-practice usability concern rather than a WCAG failure, as the link purpose is clear in context.
issues.suggestion_technical: United States (USD) with surrounding context explaining the selection.

issues.element: Multiple duplicate <h3> headings for 'Be Bold...', 'Countdown...', 'Blast Off!' and promotional links
issues.description: The heading structure across the page contains many duplicate and repeated headings, making the page outline confusing.
issues.suggestion: Use unique, descriptive headings for each section and avoid using headings purely for styling links.
issues.description_technical: The page repeats the same <h3> text multiple times and uses headings for promotional links, creating a flat, repetitive outline.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user trying to navigate by headings cannot distinguish sections because the same headings repeat.
issues.why_technical: Duplicate headings reduce the usefulness of heading navigation, which is a primary screen reader navigation strategy. NVDA/JAWS heading navigation (H key) will cycle through identical headings; VoiceOver rotor headings list will show multiple indistinguishable entries.
issues.suggestion_technical: Restructure so each content block has a unique heading; use CSS for visual styling instead of heading elements.

issues.description: An anchor in the embedded video section uses aria-level, which is not a valid attribute for links and does not make it a heading.
issues.suggestion: Use a real heading element if this is a section title, or remove aria-level if it is only a link.
issues.description_technical: aria-level is only meaningful on heading roles or structural elements; applying it to an <a> has no effect and may confuse developers.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user will not find this link in the headings list despite the aria-level hint.
issues.why_technical: Without role="heading" and aria-level together, aria-level is ignored by assistive technologies; the element remains a generic link. NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver will not include it in heading navigation, so the video title is missing from the page outline.
issues.suggestion_technical:
Video title

or remove aria-level.

issues.description: The channel avatar button in the video info section has no accessible name beyond the generic image alt text.
issues.suggestion: Add an aria-label to the button describing its action.
issues.description_technical: The button's accessible name comes only from the child image's alt ('thumbnail-image'), which is not descriptive of the button's action.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user hears 'thumbnail-image, button' and does not know it opens a channel page.
issues.why_technical: NVDA + Firefox: announces the button as 'thumbnail-image, button, clickable' without indicating the channel navigation action. JAWS 2024: the unnamed button appears in the Virtual Cursor but provides no destination context. VoiceOver iOS: rotor navigation lists 'thumbnail-image, button' with no hint that it opens a channel.
issues.suggestion_technical: <button aria-label="Go to [channel name] channel" class="ytmVideoInfoLink ytmVideoInfoChannelAvatar">...</button>

issues.description: The close button in the video player overlay contains nested interactive-looking elements and conflicting aria-labels, creating an ambiguous accessible name.
issues.suggestion: Clean up the markup and ensure the button has a single, accurate accessible name.
issues.description_technical: The button has aria-label='Close' but contains a div with aria-label='Share' and malformed attributes, risking incorrect name calculation.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user may hear 'Close' or 'Share' unpredictably, or the button may be unusable.
issues.why_technical: NVDA + Firefox: nested aria-label inside the button can override or concatenate with the outer label, producing 'Share Close, button' or 'Close Share, button'. JAWS 2024: may ignore the inner div if focusable, but malformed attributes can break the accessible name computation. VoiceOver iOS: double-tap may activate the wrong target if nested tappable elements receive separate touch events.
issues.suggestion_technical: <button aria-label="Close">...</button> with no nested aria-label or interactive elements inside.

issues.description: The main video player element has malformed attributes ('aria-hidden="', 'true"="') that will confuse browsers and assistive technologies.
issues.suggestion: Fix the video element attributes to valid HTML.
issues.description_technical: The video tag contains invalid attribute syntax, including a bare aria-hidden attribute and a stray 'true"="' attribute.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader may encounter parsing errors, causing the video or its controls to be inaccessible or behave unexpectedly.
issues.why_technical: Malformed HTML can prevent proper exposure in the accessibility tree and may break keyboard or screen reader interaction with the media player. NVDA + Firefox may drop the element from the accessibility tree; VoiceOver macOS may fail to expose the video region or its custom controls.
issues.suggestion_technical: <video playsinline webkit-playsinline tabindex="-1" aria-hidden="true">...</video>

issues.element: <button class="ytp-unmute ytp-popup ytp-button ytp-unmute-animated ytp-unmute-shrink" data-layer="2" style="display: none"></button>
issues.description: The unmute button in the video player controls has no accessible name, so screen readers announce only 'button'.
issues.suggestion: Add an aria-label or visible text to the button.
issues.description_technical: The unmute button is empty with no aria-label, aria-labelledby, or title, violating WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.2.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user cannot tell that this button unmutes the video.
issues.why_technical: NVDA + Firefox: announces 'button, clickable' with no action label. JAWS 2024: in Forms Mode the button appears as an unlabeled control. VoiceOver iOS: rotor lists 'button' without indicating unmute functionality. TalkBack: focus lands on the button but no spoken feedback describes its purpose.
issues.suggestion_technical: <button class="ytp-unmute..." aria-label="Unmute video"></button>

issues.description: The page content is not wrapped in any landmark regions such as <main>, <nav>, or <header>.
issues.suggestion: Wrap page regions in semantic landmark elements.
issues.description_technical: No ARIA landmarks or HTML5 landmark elements are used, making it impossible for screen reader users to navigate by region.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user cannot jump to the main content, navigation, or footer using landmark shortcuts.
issues.why_technical: NVDA + Firefox: landmark navigation (D key) finds no regions, forcing linear traversal. JAWS 2024: Ctrl+Insert+R/6 reports no landmarks. VoiceOver iOS: Rotor 'Headings' may be the only navigation option, with no 'Landmarks' menu. TalkBack: local context menus cannot jump to main or navigation regions.
issues.suggestion_technical: Use <header>, <nav aria-label="Primary">, <main>, and <footer> to structure the page.

issues.element: Multiple repeated content blocks (promotions, navigation, images)
issues.description: The page repeats large blocks of content and links, creating a very long focus order and reading experience.
issues.suggestion: Remove duplicate content blocks or provide a way to skip repeated sections.
issues.description_technical: Repeated DOM structures (three full sets of promotional cards and duplicated navigation) extend the tab and reading order unnecessarily.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader or keyboard user must navigate through the same content multiple times, which is tedious and disorienting.
issues.why_technical: Excessive repeated content increases the number of focusable/reading stops and can make it hard to locate unique content. Switch Access users must step through every duplicate stop sequentially.
issues.suggestion_technical: Consolidate repeated promotional blocks and ensure each link appears only once in the logical reading order.

issues.element: Multiple malformed elements: '<div <form="" ...>', '<svg aria-hidden=" focusable="false" ... true"="">', '<button aria-disabled=" title="">', '<a href=" title="MarsCommuter®">', '<video aria-hidden=" ... true"="">'
issues.description: [SYSTEMIC PATTERN] The HTML contains numerous malformed tags and attributes across at least 5+ elements, indicating a systemic templating or serialization problem that will cause parsing errors.
issues.suggestion: Validate and repair all malformed HTML throughout the document.
issues.description_technical: Multiple elements have invalid attribute syntax (e.g., '<div <form="">', 'true"=""', unclosed quotes), violating WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.1.
issues.why_simple: Browsers and screen readers may render or announce the page unpredictably, breaking navigation and interaction.
issues.why_technical: Malformed HTML can prevent proper construction of the DOM and accessibility tree, leading to missing or misrepresented elements. NVDA + Firefox and JAWS 2024 may drop malformed controls from the accessibility tree; VoiceOver iOS may misidentify regions due to broken SVG and video markup.
issues.suggestion_technical: Run the HTML through a validator and fix all syntax errors, ensuring all attributes are properly quoted and elements are correctly nested.

issues.description: A link in the page content has an empty query parameter and no accessible text, making its destination and purpose unknown.
issues.suggestion: Remove the link if it is not needed, or add descriptive text and a valid destination.
issues.description_technical: The link href ends with '?a=' and contains no text or accessible name, violating WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.4.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user cannot determine what this link does or where it goes.
issues.why_technical: NVDA + Firefox: announces 'link' with no name and exposes the raw URL. JAWS 2024: may read the href as the link text, which is not descriptive. VoiceOver iOS: rotor lists an unnamed link, making it indistinguishable from other empty links.
issues.suggestion_technical: Return to homepage or remove the element.

issues.element: Mars Commuter Express Terms and Conditions
issues.description: A link in the terms section contains a likely typo in the URL parameter ('tersm_and_conditions'), which may indicate a broken or incorrect destination.
issues.suggestion: Verify and correct the URL parameter.
issues.description_technical: The href parameter appears misspelled ('tersm' instead of 'terms'), which may lead to a non-functional or unexpected destination.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user following the link may end up on the wrong page or an error page.
issues.why_technical: Typographical errors in URL parameters can break routing and confuse users who rely on link text matching destination behavior. However, the visible link text is descriptive, so the purpose is clear in context.
issues.suggestion_technical: Mars Commuter Express Terms and Conditions

issues.description: Links in the video playlist open content in a named iframe/target without warning, which may disorient screen reader users.
issues.suggestion: Add descriptive text or aria-label explaining the link loads a video in the player.
issues.description_technical: Links with target='player' load content into an iframe without indicating that context will change in a separate region.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user may not realize that activating the link changes video content elsewhere on the page.
issues.why_technical: Unexpected context changes can confuse users; providing an indication of the behavior helps users anticipate the outcome. VoiceOver iOS: focus typically remains on the link after activation, so the user receives no feedback that the player region updated.
issues.suggestion_technical: Why Mars died

issues.description: The main page heading 'Destination Mars' uses very light text color (#eee) which may fail contrast, and the page has multiple sets of headings that do not form a coherent outline.
issues.suggestion: Restructure headings into a single coherent outline and ensure sufficient color contrast.
issues.description_technical: While the color contrast issue is visual, the heading structure is fragmented with repeated h3s and promotional links as headings.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user navigating by headings finds a confusing, repetitive outline rather than a clear page structure.
issues.why_technical: NVDA + Firefox: heading navigation (H key) cycles through repetitive promotional headings. JAWS 2024: Insert+F6 headings list shows duplicated or skipped levels. VoiceOver iOS: Rotor headings menu becomes cluttered with non-unique promotional headings.
issues.suggestion_technical: Use one <h1>, followed by <h2> for major sections and <h3> for subsections, with unique text for each.

issues.description: [SYSTEMIC PATTERN] Multiple search inputs share the same name="query" and there are duplicate id="id-country-preference" values, indicating a systemic duplication of form controls that can break label associations and form submission.
issues.suggestion: Make all id and name values unique where they represent distinct controls.
issues.description_technical: The document contains multiple <input name="query"> elements and at least two elements with id="id-country-preference". Duplicate IDs violate HTML validity and WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.1, and break aria-labelledby/for associations.
issues.why_simple: Assistive technology and browsers may get confused about which field or checkbox is being referenced, leading to wrong labels being announced or actions applied to the wrong control.
issues.why_technical: IDs must be unique within a document. Duplicate IDs cause getElementById and accessibility APIs to return unpredictable results, breaking label associations and scripting. NVDA + Firefox: label click may move focus to the first duplicate; JAWS 2024: Forms Mode may associate the wrong label with the second search field.
issues.suggestion_technical: Use unique ids such as search-query-1, search-query-2, and country-preference-1, country-preference-2, or remove duplicate form controls from the DOM.

issues.description: The search region div has a malformed attribute "<form=""" which creates invalid HTML and may break the form structure.
issues.suggestion: Fix the malformed markup and use proper semantic form elements.
issues.description_technical: The attribute <form="" on the <div> is not valid HTML and indicates broken markup. This can cause assistive technology and browsers to parse the page incorrectly, violating WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.1.
issues.why_simple: Screen readers and other tools may not recognize the form region correctly, making it harder to navigate and use.
issues.why_technical: Invalid markup can cause the accessibility tree to be built incorrectly, leading to missing or misrepresented form regions and controls. NVDA + Firefox: the search region may not be exposed as a form landmark; JAWS 2024: may fail to recognize the region as a search form.
issues.suggestion_technical: Remove the invalid <form="" attribute. If a form wrapper is intended, use <form id="search"> with a proper opening tag and matching </form>.

issues.description: The search input in the search region is missing an autocomplete attribute that could help users fill it in.
issues.suggestion: Add an autocomplete attribute to the search field.
issues.description_technical: The search field collects query text but lacks an autocomplete attribute. While search is not strictly a personal data field under WCAG 1.3.5, adding autocomplete="search" improves predictability and user-agent support.
issues.why_simple: Users with cognitive or motor disabilities benefit when browsers can predict and fill in common search terms.
issues.why_technical: The autocomplete attribute allows user agents to programmatically identify the input purpose, supporting fill-in and personalization features. Real-world impact is limited for a generic search field because search queries are rarely personal data stored by browsers.
issues.suggestion_technical: Add autocomplete="search" to the search input.

issues.description: A 1x1 tracking pixel in the page footer has no alt attribute, so screen readers may announce the filename or image role without meaning.
issues.suggestion: Mark the tracking pixel as decorative.
issues.description_technical: The 1x1 tracking pixel lacks an alt attribute. Because it conveys no content, it should be marked as decorative with alt="".
issues.why_simple: A blind user may hear the image filename or be told an image exists without knowing it is meaningless.
issues.why_technical: NVDA + Firefox: may announce the image as 'graphic seg' or read the filename. JAWS 2024: may announce 'image seg' in Virtual Cursor. VoiceOver iOS: may report 'image' with no useful description. Adding alt="" removes it from the accessibility tree.

issues.description: An image in the content area has alt text that does not match the image it describes.
issues.suggestion: Update the alt text to describe the actual image.
issues.description_technical: The alt text describes a baboon, but the src is mars-sunrise.jpg. Mismatched alt text misrepresents the image content.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user is told the image shows a baboon when it actually shows a Martian sunrise.
issues.why_technical: NVDA + Firefox: announces 'Beautiful baboon, blowing bubbles, biking backward, graphic' while the visible image is a Martian sunrise. JAWS 2024: reads the incorrect alt text, misleading the user about the image content. VoiceOver iOS: describes the image using the wrong alt text.

issues.description: The channel avatar button in the video info section has no accessible name beyond a generic image alt.
issues.suggestion: Give the button a clear accessible name via aria-label.
issues.description_technical: The button's accessible name comes from the child image's alt text "thumbnail-image", which is not descriptive of the button's action.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user cannot tell that this button opens the channel page or profile.
issues.why_technical: NVDA + Firefox: announces the element as 'thumbnail-image, button, clickable' without action context. JAWS 2024: the button is reachable but unnamed in terms of purpose. VoiceOver iOS: rotor lists 'thumbnail-image, button' with no indication it navigates to a channel.

issues.element: <button aria-label="Close" class="ytSpecButtonShapeNextHost ytSpecButtonShapeNextText ytSpecButtonShapeNextOverlay ytSpecButtonShapeNextSizeM ytSpecButtonShapeNextIconOnlyDefault" data-closest-spacing="0" data-rendered-height="30" data-rendered-width="40" title="">
issues.description: The close button in the video player overlay has an empty title attribute that may override or conflict with its aria-label.
issues.suggestion: Remove the empty title attribute to keep the accessible name clear.
issues.description_technical: The button has aria-label="Close" but title="". An empty title can suppress tooltips but should not be relied upon; ensure the accessible name remains "Close".
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user may hear an unexpected or empty name if the title attribute interferes with the aria-label.
issues.why_technical: Accessible name calculation prioritizes aria-label over title, so the name remains 'Close' in modern browsers. The empty title is redundant and has minimal real-world impact, though it is unnecessary markup.
issues.suggestion_technical: <button aria-label="Close" ...></button>

issues.description: A disabled button in the video player overlay has malformed attributes and no accessible name, making it unusable for assistive technology.
issues.suggestion: Fix the markup and provide an accessible name and explicit disabled state.
issues.description_technical: The button tag is malformed (aria-disabled=" title="") and contains only an aria-hidden icon, so it has no accessible name or clear disabled state.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user cannot tell what the button does or whether it is disabled.
issues.why_technical: NVDA + Firefox: announces 'button' with no name and may not expose a disabled state due to the malformed aria-disabled attribute. JAWS 2024: in Forms Mode the control appears unnamed and its state is unclear. VoiceOver iOS: the button is focusable but provides no action or state information.

issues.description: A link in the page content has no text content, so its purpose is invisible to screen reader users.
issues.suggestion: Add visible link text or an aria-label describing the link purpose.
issues.description_technical: The anchor element is empty and has no aria-label or title. WCAG 2.4.4 requires link purpose to be determinable from the link text alone or in context.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user hears only "link" with no indication it leads to an email action.
issues.why_technical: NVDA + Firefox: announces 'link' and may read the raw URL. JAWS 2024: may announce the href as link text, which is not meaningful. VoiceOver iOS: rotor lists an unnamed link. TalkBack: swipe navigation lands on the link but provides no spoken purpose.
issues.suggestion_technical: ...

issues.description: [SYSTEMIC PATTERN] Multiple navigation links are empty, so their destinations cannot be understood by screen reader users. This pattern appears across several <a class="link"> elements in the page navigation, indicating a missing rule for ensuring link text or aria-label in the design system.
issues.suggestion: Add descriptive text or aria-labels to each empty navigation link.
issues.description_technical: Several <a class="link"> elements have no text or accessible name. These appear to be navigation links whose purpose is hidden from assistive technology.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user navigating by links hears only "link" repeatedly and cannot choose where to go.
issues.why_technical: Empty anchors produce empty accessible names, breaking the link list rotor and tab navigation for screen reader users. NVDA + Firefox: announces only "link" with no action label; JAWS 2024: lists the link as blank in the Links Virtual Buffer; VoiceOver iOS: rotor shows an unnamed link; TalkBack: swipe navigation reaches a link with no spoken label.
issues.suggestion_technical: Why MarsCommuter

issues.element: Get your free dehydrated ice cream!
issues.description: Duplicate link text points to different URLs, which can confuse screen reader users.
issues.suggestion: Ensure each link has unique, descriptive text or use aria-label to distinguish links with the same visible text.
issues.description_technical: The text "Get your free dehydrated ice cream!" and similar promotional phrases may repeat across links with different query parameters or destinations, making link purpose ambiguous.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user browsing the links list may select the wrong link because the same text leads to different pages.
issues.why_technical: Screen reader users often navigate by a rotor of links; duplicate link text with different hrefs creates ambiguity. NVDA + Firefox: Links List shows multiple identical entries; JAWS 2024: Insert+F7 links list cannot distinguish duplicates; VoiceOver iOS: rotor groups identical labels, forcing linear exploration.
issues.suggestion_technical: Get your free dehydrated ice cream!

issues.element: Send your kids to mars
issues.description: Duplicate link text with different destinations appears for the same topic.
issues.suggestion: Make link text unique or add aria-label to clarify each link's purpose.
issues.description_technical: The text "Send your kids to mars" appears on links with different closest-spacing and possibly different contexts, but the same href. However, other links with the same visible text may point to different URLs elsewhere on the page.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user may be unsure which link to activate when the same text appears multiple times with different destinations.
issues.why_technical: Duplicate visible link text reduces the effectiveness of link navigation for assistive technology users. NVDA + Firefox: Links List shows identical entries; JAWS 2024: links list cannot differentiate duplicates; VoiceOver iOS: rotor groups identical labels.
issues.suggestion_technical: Send your kids to mars

issues.description: A video title link in the video section is empty, so its destination is unknown to screen reader users. The invalid aria-level attribute on the anchor also misrepresents the element as a heading.
issues.suggestion: Add the video title as link text and remove aria-level from the anchor.
issues.description_technical: The anchor has aria-level="2" but no text content or aria-label. The aria-level attribute is not valid on an <a> element and does not provide an accessible name.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user cannot tell which video this link opens.
issues.why_technical: aria-level is intended for heading roles, not links. The empty anchor yields no accessible name, making the link purpose unknown. NVDA + Firefox: announces "link" with no name; JAWS 2024: skips or reports blank link; VoiceOver iOS: rotor lists an unnamed link; TalkBack: reaches a link with no spoken label.
issues.suggestion_technical: Life was possible on Mars

issues.description: A video thumbnail link in the video gallery stores its visible label in a data attribute rather than as accessible text, so screen readers cannot announce "Why Mars died".
issues.suggestion: Move the data-text value into the anchor content or an aria-label.
issues.description_technical: The link text "Why Mars died" is in data-text but not in the anchor's text content or aria-label. Screen readers will not announce it unless JavaScript copies it.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user may hear an empty or filename-based link name instead of "Why Mars died".
issues.why_technical: data-* attributes are not exposed to assistive technologies as accessible names; the link needs visible text or an aria-label. NVDA + Firefox: announces the URL or "link" only; JAWS 2024: may read the href filename; VoiceOver iOS: rotor shows an unnamed or URL-named link; TalkBack: swipe navigation reaches a link with no meaningful label.
issues.suggestion_technical: Why Mars died

issues.description: The country selector link in the page header is empty and has no accessible name, so screen reader users cannot identify its purpose.
issues.suggestion: Add an accessible name to the country selector link.
issues.description_technical: The anchor with id="id-country-selector" has no text, aria-label, or title, so its purpose is unavailable to assistive technology.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user cannot tell this link opens a country selector.
issues.why_technical: An empty anchor produces an empty accessible name, failing WCAG 2.4.4. NVDA + Firefox: announces "link" with no name; JAWS 2024: reports blank link; VoiceOver iOS: rotor shows unnamed link; TalkBack: swipe navigation reaches a link with no spoken label.
issues.suggestion_technical: Select your country

issues.description: A video gallery link opens a video player in a named target frame without warning.
issues.suggestion: Indicate in the link text that the link loads a video player.
issues.description_technical: Links with target="player" load content into a named frame. Users should be informed when a link changes context by loading media in a target frame.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user may be surprised when a video starts playing in a different part of the page.
issues.why_technical: Opening content in a target frame changes the browsing context; warning users helps them anticipate the behavior. This is a AAA criterion with limited real-world enforcement; impact is lower than missing link names.
issues.suggestion_technical: Why Mars died (loads video player)

issues.description: [SYSTEMIC PATTERN] Multiple identical headings such as "Be Bold...", "Countdown...", and "Blast Off!" are used as promotional labels rather than section markers, weakening the heading outline across the page.
issues.suggestion: Use headings only to introduce content sections; use other styling for promotional phrases.
issues.description_technical: Headings such as "Be Bold...", "Countdown...", and "Blast Off!" are repeated and used as promotional labels rather than section markers. This weakens the heading outline.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user trying to skim the page by headings hears repeated, generic labels that do not describe sections.
issues.why_technical: Headings should describe the topic or purpose of the content they introduce; using them as stylistic labels misrepresents document structure. NVDA + Firefox: Heading navigation (H) lands on promotional phrases; JAWS 2024: Insert+F6 headings list becomes cluttered with non-section labels; VoiceOver iOS: rotor headings list loses utility.
issues.suggestion_technical:
Be Bold...

instead of

Be Bold...

issues.description: [SYSTEMIC PATTERN] Headings are used to style promotional links rather than structure content. Multiple <h3> elements contain only promotional links, turning the heading hierarchy into a link list.
issues.suggestion: Remove heading tags from promotional links and style them as regular links or list items.
issues.description_technical: Multiple <h3> elements contain only promotional links. This turns the heading hierarchy into a link list and obscures the page structure.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user navigating by headings finds mostly promotional links instead of content sections.
issues.why_technical: Headings should mark sections of content; wrapping every link in a heading degrades the semantic outline. NVDA + Firefox: Heading list is dominated by promo links; JAWS 2024: Insert+F6 headings list becomes a link list; VoiceOver iOS: rotor headings list loses structural meaning.
issues.suggestion_technical: 10% off Crater Adventure

issues.element: <input class="search" data-closest-spacing="4" data-rendered-height="21" data-rendered-width="158" name="query" placeholder="search" type="text"/>
issues.description: The search input in the top header has no associated <label>, so screen reader users may not know its purpose.
issues.suggestion: Add a visible <label> or an aria-label to each search input.
issues.description_technical: The search text inputs use only a placeholder attribute. Placeholders are not persistent labels and do not satisfy WCAG 1.3.1/3.3.2 labeling requirements.
issues.why_simple: A screen reader user may not realize the field is for searching once the placeholder disappears or is not announced consistently.
issues.why_technical: Accessible name calculation may use placeholder, but it is not a reliable substitute for a <label> or aria-label. NVDA + Firefox: may announce placeholder as name inconsistently; JAWS 2024: placeholder may not be announced in Forms Mode; VoiceOver iOS: placeholder may be silent after focus; TalkBack: editable field may lack a spoken role/purpose.
issues.suggestion_technical: <label for="search-query">Search</label><input id="search-query" class="search" name="query" type="text"/>
